title: Gari Biscuits
author: Marvellina
desc: A cup each of gari and plain flour with cold butter cut in to coarse crumbs — twelve to fifteen minutes until golden brown, and they keep two weeks.
longDesc: Gari biscuits turn the cassava staple into a sweet, and the method is a straightforward rubbed-in biscuit dough: a cup of gari flour, a cup of plain flour, a teaspoon of baking soda, half a cup of sugar, a quarter teaspoon of salt, one large egg and four tablespoons of cold diced butter, with a teaspoon of water or milk if it is dry. Cut the butter into coarse crumbs, add the egg, divide into twenty pieces, flatten and bake at 350 degrees Fahrenheit twelve to fifteen minutes until golden brown. They keep up to two weeks.
ingredients: 1 tsp water or milk, as needed
steps: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
Combine the gari flour, plain flour, baking soda, sugar and salt.
Cut in the cold diced butter to coarse crumbs.
Add the egg, with a teaspoon of water or milk if the mixture is dry.
Divide into 20 pieces and flatten each one.
Bake 12 to 15 minutes, or until golden brown.
Cool 1 minute on the tray, then transfer.
chefTips: Cold butter, cut in to coarse crumbs. Warm butter gives a tough biscuit; the coarse crumb is what keeps them short.
A teaspoon of liquid only if the dough is dry. Gari is very thirsty but the egg usually does the work.
Twelve to fifteen minutes until golden brown. Gari browns readily, so check at twelve.
Cool one minute on the tray before moving them — they firm up as they cool and will break if lifted hot.
They keep up to two weeks, which makes them a genuinely useful thing to bake.

This is a modern butter-and-plain-flour bake rather than a documented traditional Ghanaian sweet, and that is worth knowing — the author calls it a Ghanaian gari biscuit but the tradition behind it could not be verified.
Equal volumes of gari and plain flour by cup, but note the gram figures differ — 160 g against 150 g — because gari is denser.
commonMistakes: Adding liquid before testing whether the egg is enough.
Moving them off the tray while hot.
Assuming it is a documented traditional recipe.
sources: Adapted from 'How To Make Gari Biscuits (African Cassava Biscuits)', whattocooktoday.com, no date shown. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Marvellina' — FIRST NAME ONLY. Quantities confirmed across two fetches and were identical (TWO-PASS). Yield as printed: 20 biscuits, 30 minutes total.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 cup gari flour (160 gr); 1 cup all-purpose flour (150 gr) — the page prints 'four' for 'flour'; 1 tsp baking soda; ½ cup sugar (100 gr); ¼ tsp salt; 1 large egg; 4 Tbsp cold butter (65 gr), diced; 1 tsp water or milk as needed. The gram conversions are as printed, including 4 tablespoons of butter at 65 g.

Method as printed: preheat 350 F; combine the dry ingredients; cut in the butter to coarse crumbs; add the egg, with a teaspoon of liquid if dry; 20 pieces, flatten; bake '12-15 minutes or until golden brown'; cool 1 minute on the tray. Keeps 'up to 2 weeks'.
DONENESS CUE, as printed: 'until golden brown', within a 12-to-15-minute window.

AN ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT, stated plainly: the author calls this a 'Ghanaian gari biscuit' but it is A MODERN BUTTER-AND-PLAIN-FLOUR BAKE and its standing as a Ghanaian tradition COULD NOT BE VERIFIED from any other source. It is published because it is a quantified, cue-bearing use of gari by a named author, and the uncertainty about its traditional status is flagged rather than hidden.

NOT GA, and a different product: Yawo A.M., 'Fortification of cassava starch biscuit in Agbozume', University of Education Winneba, 2015, documents a VOLTA REGION cassava-STARCH biscuit, which is not the same thing as a gari biscuit. It is recorded so the two are not conflated.

ON GARI ITSELF: its production is a fermentation and is NOT published in this collection. Whitby 1968, the CSIR bulletin, describes it: 'Peeled fresh cassava is grated rather more coarsely than for dough. It is put in a sack and weights are placed on it to squeeze out the juice. During this time it partly ferments. Sqeezing may continue for two or three days.' — 'Sqeezing' as printed. That was REFUSED under the fermentation rule, because 'partly ferments' over two or three days carries no observable endpoint. Gari therefore appears throughout this collection only as a bought ingredient.
storage: Up to 2 weeks in an airtight tin, per the author.
reheating: Not needed. A few minutes in a low oven crisps them again.
healthBenefits: Lower in gluten than an all-wheat biscuit.
Modest sugar at half a cup across twenty biscuits.
culturalNote: Gari is cheap, keeps forever and turns up in everything from a cold drink to a biscuit, which is the mark of a true staple. Whether this particular biscuit is traditional or a diaspora invention could not be established, and it is published with that question left open rather than answered either way.
